newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA STABILISES BANKS AFTER INSOLVENCIES.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA STABILISES BANKS AFTER INSOLVENCIES.

text.p: Bulgaria is taking steps to stabilise its banking system through privatisations and tighter financial discipline after a wave of insolvencies last year, officials said on Wednesday.

Bulgaria sealed its first bank privatisation deal on Tuesday, selling 99.6 percent of United Bulgarian Bank to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), Bulgaria's Bulbank and the U.S. Oppenheimer & Co. Inc.

"The first sale of a Bulgarian bank is a signal to the international banking community that the government is keen to complete its bank restructuring programme," said Dimitar Dimitrov, acting director of the Bank Consolidation Company (BCC), which manages state equity in commercial banks and is involved in talks with potential buyers.
The same day, the Sofia City Court declared an eighth bank bankrupt on the basis of an insolvency claim filed by the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB).
Lack of central control on banks which sprang up after the end of communist rule enabled them to make uncollateralised loans and to siphon large sums abroad for powerful clients.

A report last year by parliament's committee on corruption cited a company which used 2.5 million live fish in a reservoir as collateral for a $4 million credit from Sirbank, which merged with other banks in 1995.
Reforms are inevitable now because the currency board regime introduced on July 1 bans lending from the central bank to commercial banks except in cases of systemic risk.
In line with the pledges to the International Monetary Fund Bulgaria plans to privatise its remaining five operating state-owned banks by mid-1998.
Dimitrov said Austria's Raiffeisenbank and South Korea's Daewoo Corp were potential buyers for Varna-based Expressbank and the BCC had invited them to place bids on a competive basis by August 20.
The BCC plans to come up with sell-off plans for the Bulgarian Post Bank and Plovdiv-based Hebrosbank by the beginning of September.

The privatisation of Biochim Bank, recently stabilised through government support, will follow a different procedure. After Bulgaria failed to seal a management contract with the Dutch ABN Amro the BCC sent letters to 25 international banks offering Biochim for urgent privatisation.
A sell-off scheme for Bulbank, Bulgaria's largest state commercial bank with assets of $2.4 billion at end-1996, has not been announced yet.

Since May 1996, the BNB has sought insolvency through the courts for 17 state and private banks, a third of the country's total. Eight have been ruled insolvent so far and the BNB has withdrawn insolvency claims against two more after buyers were found -- for Mollovbank, now renamed Eurobank, and for Yambol Bank, renamed Bulgaria Invest Commercial Bank.
Once the cases make their way through the courts, the authorities must consider compensating savers, though a sharp fall in the lev means frozen deposits are worth far less than they were last year.
To minimise credit risks, the BNB plans to speed up banks' compliance with capital adequacy criteria agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said a BNB official.
"The BNB is planning to require local banks to reach a capital to risk assets ratio of eight percent by end-1997, half a year earlier than agreed with the IMF," he said.

Bulgaria agreed with the IMF earlier this year to boost capital adequacy ratios for local banks to six percent by end-1997, eight percent by mid-1998, 10 percent by end-1998 and 12 percent by end-1999.

"It is logical to ask healthy banks to speed up raising their capital to risk assets ratio because their liquidity rose substantially prior to the introduction of the currency board system thanks to repo operations with the central bank and short-term government securities issues," said the BNB official.
